The question had been: Mr. Hubo, you have explained in the procedure for assigning resources including facilities. And we have discussed the El Mujahedin Detachment, was the competent body, the Municipal Defence Secretariat, that determined these issues a military body or a civilian body? Your answer was: The municipal organ decided whether -- I can't read this English here. To mobilised whether there was such need -- I don't know what was typed here, not the military organ. They sent requests for that. In this particular incident there and there are some words missing, military unit earlier on and probably it remained requisitioned once the unit left. I believe that it had the status of having been requisitioned since 1992 and this municipal organ merely established that the facility had indeed been requisitioned whereas this other part, this other -- now again, I can't read there word, had been used, had not been formally requisitioned and therefore it speaks of this subsequent request and the need to submit it in order for the facility to be formally requisitioned. Perhaps this is confusing, but can you see this is the 17th of June 1995 and a great many things happened since 1992, I believe, that the facility had been requisitioned as early as 1992, but I can't tell you this with precision because I don't have records. I suppose that when the unit took up this facility it was merely the user of the facility that changed but the status of the facility remained the same. Now, obviously a number of words have been misspelled in the answer, and some of them have been left out. The answer is to me incomprehensible. But if this does help you to remind you of what you were trying to say, I would appreciate it if you could repeat yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Let me state that I find it difficult to repeat my answer since I didn't learn them by heart, to meet your request I do want to be as fair as possible and repeat. This is a very wide discussion and a deal of it is speculation. I can tell you what I know. On the basis of this document I can tell you that the commission established the status of the requisitioned facility. What I can speculate on the basis of this, if you will agree with me, I think, I don't have a document, that this facility, the Vatrostalna facility had been requisitioned earlier on for the purposes of one of the units of the armed forces which had in the meantime or left somewhere, I don't know whether it happened with it. As for this other facility, the Apatinska Pivara facility, had never been requisitioned, and they established this in the document and the secretariat asked that the unit submit a request so that the facility can indeed be requisitioned and handed over to them for use as was legally proper. This was the sort of procedure conducted by the Municipal Defence Secretariat for which the secretariat was responsible. The units submitted their needs in writing to the secretariat, and the secretariat, in turn, examined what the options were and on the basis of the conclusion of that assessment, they -- the secretariat either requisitioned the sort of goods or not and of course on this -- it was on this that their meeting or not meeting of the requests from units depended. I don't know if I've managed to answer your question fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic can tell us that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This time the interpretation is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now just clear me on one little point, Mr. Hubo, where do you get it from, looking -- by looking at this document, that Vatrostalna had been requisitioned for purposes of another unit before and where you get that from because I'm not picking that up by looking at the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can conclude this based on my memory, because many units in that period were established and then disbanded, they came and went; and I can't tell you whether this was actually the truth, but I think that this particular facility had been in use much earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's something you remember from knowledge -- your knowledge of what happened then, not something you're picking up from the document, this document before us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document only states that the appropriated facility, that it should be -- that it is being utilized properly, it doesn't say when. But based on the document, this is what I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess I can't take the matter any further. Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robson. Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologize, it was a D document, I missed that. Could I ask for the document to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May document 999 please be given an exhibit number. The document is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours this will become exhibit number 1315.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Hubo, my name is Kyle Wood, and I represent the Prosecution in this case. I will be asking you some questions now. Now, first off, Mr. Hubo, I just want to understand the context and make sure that the Trial Chamber understands the context of your testimony today. Now, you told us that you took up your duties in the organ for organisation, mobilisation, and personnel affairs in September 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: September 1993 is when the takeover started. It took a while, several months, actually. It lasted several months for the entire takeover to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: You were there for several months. In fact, you were there until the end of the war. This is the same position that you held. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name changed, the number of employees, but, in fact, this organ existed until the end of the war, and it dealt with these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And this was essentially a 3rd Corps headquarters organ. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a 3rd Corps command organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And, again, I don't think you answered my question about how long you remained in this organ. You said that it existed to the end of the war, and it dealt with these issues. You, in fact, were the head of that organ from 1993 until the end of the war. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. But I just stress again, that the organ changed the name, and the number of people working for it changed. At some point there were nine men working, at another point there were 13 men working in the organ itself, but I remained at the head of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So, for example, you never became a brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never became a brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: You were a never a battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was never a battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And in your position, difficult though it was, you weren't in any position to issue any combat orders to any units in the 3rd Corps. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I prepared and issued orders in my capacity as the Chief of Staff, and the commanders would sign those.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So you didn't issue combat orders for example, that is, to sign them during operations Proljece or Farz?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have the competence to do something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I want to clear up one other thing. You said that you joined this organ in September 1993. That was after the order for the formation of the El Mujahid Detachment had already been issued by General Delic. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So you weren't there when General Delic issued the order forming the El Mujahid Detachment?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't, not in this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And generally, Mr. Hubo, you've told the Trial Chamber that military records are important for determining whether somebody was a member of the army. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it is correct. You have to have records of everything that is happening and that also includes the conscript records.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And you told us, for example, that there were women in Vitez who fought in the liberation war but they did not have status as members of the army because the correct lists weren't drawn up. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's partly correct. It's not just about lists. It's also about keeping records of them. Records within an official organ that is supposed to keep the records and within whose competence it is. So if you weren't mobilised by a competent organ or you were not on the list of a unit that was established, then you are not a member of the army. And if you were on a list or in the records of that unit, then by this fact alone already, you would earn the status of member. So if a woman was not on file within a unit, then she wouldn't have that status.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If your name is on a list in the records of that unit, then by this fact alone you would earn status of a member. Is that your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a unit kept a record of you being on their list that means that you had the status of being a member of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, we've heard a lot of testimony over the last couple of days about the Municipal Secretariats. You told the Trial Chamber that the lists that were drawn up had to be sent to the Municipal Secretariats. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me about volunteers or about something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'm talking about the formation of any unit.

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any unit, if a mobilisation was carried out in the normal course, in the normal manner that would be reported to the secretariat. Once the conscript reported to the unit command, the unit would make a record of it, they call his information, and in the end it would compile a list and forward it to the Defence Secretariats, so that they could compare their files.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And those records were kept by the individual unit and by the municipal secretariat. Is that your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The records had to be kept within each independent unit and almost identical records were also in the secretariats.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The municipal secretariats, you mentioned, I think, just at the end of your testimony that those were civilian organs. Didn't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were civilian administrative organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And you were in the ARBiH from 1993 until 1995? Or, actually, I believe you still are.

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're not right. I was in the ARBiH from 1992 to 1995, then I was in the army of the federation and now I'm a member of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina, so this is different, in effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification, sir. You're certainly not a part of the municipal secretariats in 1993, 1994, or 1995?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I already said that this was a civilian organ, an administrative organ that was there side by side in addition to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And again, we've established that it was up to the secretariats to keep the lists and the individual units. In fact, sir, it wasn't really the responsibility of the corps command to keep any of these lists. Isn't that correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, my learned friend referred to lists. We've established that it was up to the secretariats to keep the lists. But the witness's testimony has been that its records had to be kept within each independent unit and almost identical records which were also in the secretariats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So that question you're objecting to actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes its has been put as lists and that is not what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It does and the individual units. We have established that it was up to the secretariat to keep the lists and the individual units. Line 8 of page 54 [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Certain there has been a mischaracterisation or if there's been a problem with the way the witness answered, Mr. Robson is free to explore that and to correct that if there has been an error on redirect. utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but at the same time when a mischaracterisation does take place I think it is well within his right to say, Sorry that's not what the witness said. The witness said this and I think let's try to keep to the correct characterisation of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So again, Mr. Hubo, it was up to the municipal secretariats to keep these records, or lists, data, as it wasn't the responsibility of the 3rd Corps command to keep these sorts of records or data or lists --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. It doesn't help to keep saying records or data or lists. Are they records, are they lists, are they data. Give them one characterisation, sir. There has been an objection to one characterisation which you keep persisting on, so make your mind what up what characterisation you're going to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I think data, Your Honour, would cover it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: As you please, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So we will try again, Mr. Hubo. It was up to the Municipal Secretariats in the individual units to keep this data. It wasn't up to the 3rd Corps to keep this data. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, the term that was used wasn't clear. utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: You also told the Trial Chamber that you were informed by the secretariat that they never received information but you didn't have any firsthand knowledge about whether the El Mujahid Detachment gave any data to the Municipal Secretariats. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: My question was, sir, you had no direct firsthand knowledge about whether the EMD submitted any data to the Municipal Secretariats.

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the information on the basis of information I received from the municipal secretariat. This was firsthand information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Hubo, you've told us earlier just in your -- in response to a question that I put that records are important in determining the status of membership in the army. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. The records were key to establishing the factual situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Isn't it true that another way of telling whether some -- a particular soldier was a member of the ABiH is whether that was person was paid or compensated for his activities?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean military pay or generally?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Well, you wouldn't pay somebody as a soldier unless they were actually a soldier in the army. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one point in time the army did begin to pay their soldiers. There were occasions, situations, where a person was a member of the army, but his company actually paid him because the army did not pay him. There were those situations where companies or firms where people used to work that they paid and assisted these people financially. But it was the responsible of the army to ensure that they get paid.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And military records were important in determining whether and how much somebody would be paid. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the moment when the military personnel received their pay from the army, I can't tell you exactly when this was, but the finance organs, they received lists from the secretariats of who the members of units were and based on these, these people were paid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to my colleague if we can just correct the transcript because a portion of the answer that the witness gave is missing, and it is creating confusion. utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you can, Mr. Wood. I'm lost, because page 58 starts with Madam Vidovic speaking on my screen, so when she refers to page 58, line 12, I don't know which part is it, line 12 is on page 57 for me. At one point in time, the army did begin to pay the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, Your Honour, page 57.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Line 12. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I would suggest that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem is that nobody is waiting for everybody to be done with the translation and you speak -- the interpreter can almost not even breathe anymore because everyone is speaking so fast and not making any breaks between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is true. That point is taken, Judge, and I think the parties are warned then to please be aware of that. But, Mr. Wood, I said I'm lost as to where the misinterpretation took place, but maybe the best way to deal with this is to ask the witness to answer the question once again, that was put to him at line 10 of page 57: Well, you wouldn't pay somebody as a soldier unless they were actually a soldier in the army. And let me warn you, the shorter your answers, the easier it will be to repeat them when you have to repeat them, and try to answer just the question as asked, don't expand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It is very difficult to give a short answer to this type of question because there are numerous situations. The question was: If someone was a member of the army, did he get paid for it, compensated for it, and I explained if a man is mobilised, if he is in an army unit, if he came from a company, a firm, he could receive pay from the company still. But it was the responsibility of the state to actually provide for the pay, the soldier's pay. At one point in time, the state began to pay military pay to the soldiers of the army, 20 to 40 marks --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise, the same sentence is being omitted again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, give us time. Stand up but keep quiet so that the interpretation gets finished. Just what Judge Lattanzi was saying now. When you speak while the interpreter is still speaking and that's why Judge Lattanzi feels, and I agree with her, they can hardly get time to breath. Make your point. You're saying the same sentence is being left out.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. If you allow me, this is the second time where the sentence the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina did not pay the soldiers. This is the second time that the interpreters is omitting this sentence, the same sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you start again there, sir, but it was the responsibility of the state to actually provide for the payment, the soldier's pay. Carry on there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The pay did not exist in the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. At one point in time, the soldiers began receiving -- being compensated for, in cash, I don't know what the amount was, 20, 40, marks this was symbolic, but the pay was done based on the lists and records provided for by the unit commands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now again the interpreter -- okay. It has been corrected. Thank you. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I note, Your Honour, the time. It is 5.17. Past time for the usual break. This would be a convenient time for me to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. We will take a break and come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If I could have Exhibit 114 brought up and shown to the witness, please. And specifically I'm interested in the witness seeing page 120. And I'll clarify it, 120 in the Bosnian, and 131 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wood, am I right to say this document is dated 16th of September, 1996?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Well, the page that was there originally, yes, Your Honour -- Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hubo, which talked a little bit about compensating soldiers for their service in the army. And you told us that it was important that a soldier would not be paid unless his name was on the proper list. If I could -- we could zoom in a little bit on the top. Yes. Now, Mr. Hubo, we have here --

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we continue, it has been brought to my attention that this exhibit was admitted confidentially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And I do apologise for not bringing that up earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And to the extent that it has now been made public, can it be redacted.

utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, you are saying P6263 is not on their list. Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would note that this isn't technically the first time this has come up. We have had transcripts from the Hadzihasanovic case which were assigned to P numbers. Those were offered into evidence, on second thought my colleague over here decided not to put those into the record because they had been read. Now, in general terms, P06263 is a document that has been signed by this individual. Before the Prosecution knew that he was going to be a witness, we didn't understand the importance this particular document. Therefore it would have been impossible for us to have added it to our exhibit list not knowing that Mr. Hubo would be testifying again. So, again, Your Honour, in the interest of fairness I think it is important that there be a general principle that documents that even though they're not on the Prosecution's exhibit list we still show to witnesses for various different reasons. Including to impeach their credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would imagine Mr. Wood, and I don't know what the practice is between the parties, but I would imagine that if then a document comes up which you suddenly feel you need to use because of particular witness is it going to be called, the obvious thing to do is to give notice to your opposite number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I did provide notice to them that had this was on our list of documents that we circulated or a list of document that we circulated are a list of documents that we indicated we would be showing to this witness on cross-examination. It is a P number that has been added when we did our search and found that it was particularly relevant because Mr. Hubo was testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what I mean. At least to when you give notice to your opposite side to say, Well to explain why it was not in your original 65 ter list in the first place, that now you realise it relates to a particular witness who they are going to call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At least just to give them some explanation as to why it was not on your list in the first place. I realise there is quite a bit of mutual disclosure between the parties in this practice and I have never been really to understand how it operates, but it seems as if this is what has been happening in this trial so far. Late documents are -- the opposite party is given notice even if it is late to say we're going use this document and it was not included in the first place because of the following reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, we're checking right now to confirm when notice of this was sent to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Again, as I said, the importance of this document could not have been apparent to the Prosecution before we got the 65 ter exhibit list from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that. I understand that. Judge Lattanzi was just adding also that in this situation you also need the authorisation of the Chamber. I'm not quite sure about that. Are you able to address that? I saw you, Mr. Robson, I'm coming to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're not actually asking that this actually be added to the 65 ter exhibit list. Certainly if we were that would require the leave of the Trial Chamber. This is something that was shown to the witness for various purposes, including for impeachment. I don't believe the rules require in this situation that we do seek leave of the Trial Chamber, though since this is the first situation in which this has arisen, certainly guidelines are welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Aren't you going ask that it be tendered into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, the difference is now that we're in the Defence phase we can't know what documents are going to be relevant and so on. We give notice as soon as we can do that, based on the 65 ter exhibit list. I will ask, I guess that this be tendered into evidence at some point. Certainly the Trial Chamber as a professional fact finder, and can give it whatever weight it sees fit, such -- as long as it meets the other required under Rule 89(C).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Robson, I was actually communicating with the security at the back there. But you can stand up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't mean to cut off my learned friend there. Your Honour, the position is that on Friday afternoon the Defence received an e-mail telling us which documents the Prosecution intended to use with this witness. On that list were seven documents which were not on the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter list. Of those seven documents two of those documents had been disclosed to us in a portion of material that related to Mr. Hubo arising from ISU searches. This document that we're discussing now is not one of those documents. So, in other words, there were five documents that the Defence got notice of for the very first time on Friday afternoon. The documents were in B/C/S and it is only today that copies translations of those documents have been supplied to the Defence. So certainly we would say that these are documents that we hadn't prior sight of. We have not had prior time to look into them, to see whether there's any authenticity issues and any other issues pertaining to them. We certainly did have the chance to discuss them with Mr. Hubo when he came to be proofed. And now we're in a situation where the Prosecution is trying to use these documents, they haven't told us the reason why they want to use the documents. Mr. Wood said he want do use them for different reason, including impeachment, so I think first of all they have to be clear as to why they are using the document and if they are just using it for credibility purposeless then what would they be trying to do with the document in due course. Would they be seeking to admit it purely just to deal with issues pertaining to credibility or would they be looking to rely upon the substance of the document, the contents, what it speaks of; so this is all unclear as well. And, Your Honour, obviously as I said at the beginning, this is an principle at stake here. Based on what we heard from Mr. Hubo I don't see any cause for the Prosecution to try and impeach his testimony in relation to certificates unless they can point out something that they can show arises from what he has told us in connection with this document, so in a nutshell, Your Honour, this is a document we say the Prosecution should not be able to rely upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just have a problem that -- the opposite side must understand completely what the other side wants to use a document for and unless you understand what they want to use it for they should not be allowed to use it. I don't understand that kind of principle and I would like to get a reference for it. As I understand it, and I'm aware of you, Mr. Mundis, if a witness is coming and a particular party wants to impeach that witness, I would imagine that you could bring any document to impeach that witness. And if you say you're using it for purposes of impeachment then of course the Trial Chamber is going to looks at it for purposes of impeachment and purposes of impeachment only, unless you give us another purpose. I think your learned friend has told you he wants to use it for purpose of impeachment and what he said various reasons including impeachment if he uses for other reasons we will see those reasons emerge. If it is impeachment only, it will be impeachment and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'm following, and I am with you to a certain extent, Your Honour. But what I would submit is that if in fact the Prosecution want to use this document for reasons other than impeachment and then I think, number one, they need to make that clear in due course. But number two, I think then a question arises to whether they should either have asked for permission to add it to the Rule 65 ter list or whether they should it make an application to do so because I think if a document is being used for reasons other than impeachment in other words a Prosecution one to rely upon the substance of it to prove their case so it goes to guilt or innocence then it could well be and we would say it is a scenario where it should be added to the Rule 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me understand you clearly. If it only used for impeachment there is no need for it to be clued in the 65 ter list. Is that what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- Your Honour, this is a tricky area and I know that the practice varies from chamber to chamber. Our simple position should be that any document should be under the Rule 65 ter list, but particularly those which don't touch on credibility issues, if I can put it that way. I know some chamber take a more relaxed view with regard to documents used to test credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your short answer if it deals with credibility it be can be admitted without being on the 65 ter list. This is what I hear you saying, if I must summarize you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'll go along with that, Your Honour. But, as I say, the Prosecution has to establish that they've got valid reasons to try and impugn a witness's credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You won't know until they impeach them. They don't have to tell you, I'm going to impeach him on this point and on that point. They say this is a document I'm going to use it for impeachment. Unless you really say they must show you the arsenal completely right at the begin, I don't know how you operate. Mr. Mundis, I know have you been standing for quite sometime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I sat down in the middle there, Your Honour, but thank you very much. I think there is a couple of points that should be made very clear. First of all, as the Presiding Judge was just alluding to, we don't know if we will be impeaching the witness with the document until he is shown the document an offered an opportunity to comment upon the document. This is a document that at least based on the face of the document was signed by the witness. But let me go to the more general point, which is as my learned colleague Mr. Robson has indicated is a question really of principle. During the Prosecution phase of this case, 432 documents were tendered by the Defence during the cross-examination of Prosecution witnesses, not a single one of those documents was on the Defence 65 ter list because at that point in time there was no such thing as a Defence 65 ter list. Similarly, the Prosecution's 65 ter list in effect, applies to documents the Prosecution will be using in the Prosecution phrase of the case. There is simply no way for to us project what documents we might be showing to Defence witnesses in the Defence phase of the case. Alternatively, we could have listed 7 or 800.000 documents on our 65 ter list in anticipation of possible documents to be used during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no way that we could have do than. There is no way any chamber would have allowed to us do that. The 65 ter list pertain to the Prosecution case, just as the Defence 65 ter list pertains to the Defence case. Now, if the Defence position is that we are only tendering documents to impeach witnesses, I would urge the Trial Chamber to take a consistent approach and with respect to the 432 documents tendered by the Defence, in cross-examining the Prosecution witnesses we would strongly suggest that those documents only be looked at for the limited purpose of impeaching the witnesses. Again it is a question to paraphrase my learned colleague from the Defence of a principle, and that principle is equality of arms for both sides, and equal rules for both sides. This is cross-examination. We don't know what the witness will say about the document. We don't know for what purpose the document may or may not be used later until the witness is shown the document and afforded an opportunity to comment upon the document, if the document is relevant and the document has probative value and the witness says, Yes this is my document, then the Trial Chamber should be allowed to consider that document on the merits of the document and for the truth of the matter contained in the document. There should simply be no false division of this document goes for this purpose or that purpose. Clearly if it is being used to impeach the witness everyone will know about that. That's not really the issue at this point in time. What we're talking about here in terms of the Defence objection about the 65 ter list, is it is simply impossible for the Prosecution to list every potential document that would be used in the Prosecution case and to be used to cross-examine Defence witnesses when we file that list before trial and we simply have no idea who, if anyone, the Defence will be calling. So I would take issue with the Defence position. I will also indicate as I said at the pre-Defence conference that the issue of documents coming up being discovered, if you will, once we run the names of the Defence witnesses and that this would likely happened I indicated at that point in time the more advance notice we had of the actual schedule of the Defence witnesses the more time the Defence would have in terms of knowing which documents our internal searchs pull up for each of the Defence witness names. I was very clear about that at the pre-Defence conference for this exact very reason. So, I would urge the Trial Chamber to reject the Defence objections and as Mr. Robson has clearly indicated and I believe Mr. Wood as well that we certainly be very helpful at this early stage of the Defence case do get some guidelines on how this type of issue will be resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as this discussion that is under way right now is on a very important issue which will probably arise as an issue in the future as well, and we expect to get instructions from the Trial Chamber on them, I would also like to touch upon a general issue outside of what the witness has been speaking of here, and give a general explanation -- actually, add on to what my colleague Mr. Mundis has said. It is it true that the Defence and the Prosecution or in fact that there is an legal principle that is applied here and that is equality of arms and this principle of course applies to both sides and that is correct. However, it is also true that the Prosecution and the Defence are not in the same position when the time for discovery or disclosure is concerned nor are they in the same position to gain insight into the documents that deal with the matters that are at the crux of the case here. Your Honour, before I can compile my 65 ter list, in other words the list that -- that the Prosecutor wants to use in his -- during his case, this preparation goes on for some five years or so. So the Prosecution has have a very long period of time to locate any such exhibits to determine what their strategy will be, and to put those exhibits on their list. In this case, we deal with a -- several thousand documents that are on this list. The case law of this Tribunal has resolved this issue clearly and my colleague Mr. Mundis is very aware of this. I will only mention two cases in which Mr. Mundis himself was involved. In the Hadzihasanovic case, and the Prlic case, the issue was raised on the use of exhibits that the Prosecutor had not included on his 65 ter list at the time during the Defence case. The Trial Chamber took a very clear position at least in these two cases, I will mention only these two because I'm aware of them, that those exhibits, those documents, may be used but only in a limited scope. In a situation where it is necessary in order to remind or refresh the memory of the witness, which is what we did so far, and also in a situation where the witness is being impugned. Your Honour, this clearly implies that the Defence must have such documents in time so that it can then use its own right arising from Article 21 of the statute, 20 and 21, in other words to have sufficient time for the preparation of its case. In this concrete situation this meant that we there was no way that this document that we received in the English version that my colleague Mr. Robson was questioning on, so we could not have this document in translation, in English an hour before the trial, we have a fundamental right to the sufficient time to prepare our case. As for this document that the Prosecution is claiming here that he should have forwarded to us, let me inform you of this, Your Honour. The Defence, in a meeting with the counsel, with the Chamber counsel, informed the Prosecutor that it -- very early on that this is a witness, witness, Mr. Hubo, who will be called and who had also testified in the Hadzihasanovic case. I'm certain that we have informed of this at least four weeks before this, and therefore let me say that offering a document like this at the last minute where we have no idea what kind of document is concerned, does it -- this does not allow us enough time to prepare. For every other case, unless it is to impugn the witness and in the event that a document was not provided in time, it is necessary to obtain the decision of the Trial Chamber that this document is can be actually used and this is the position of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you confirm or deny that the 432 documents that the Defence used in the Prosecution phase were given notice of to the Prosecution in advance by way of a 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Be very short.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, to be honest, I'm not sure that I understand your question properly. Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I will repeat it. Was a 65 ter list given in advance to the Prosecution during the Prosecution's phase of the trial of the documents that the Defence intended using to cross-examine Prosecution witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am still not clear on the meaning of your question. Are you asking me whether we have submitted to the Prosecutor -- I'm really concerned. I'm not sure that I understood the interpretation. I'm concerned about the interpretation today. But was your question -- did it mean. Could you please repeat your question one more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I will repeat myself one more time. During the Prosecution phase of this trial, did the Defence give the Prosecution advance notice by way of a 65 ter list of the documents the Defence intended using to cross-examine Prosecution witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we acted as far as the obligation of the Defence was, to inform the Prosecutor of other documents that it intends to use, we proceeded exactly in the way that the instructions -- in keeping with the instruction that the Trial Chamber issued. So if the instruction was to provide such documents two days in advance, that's what we did. But I have to repeat, the position of the Defence in that phase is not the same. Nor is the position of the Prosecutor in our phase the same as ours in their phase. Nor is the accused in the same position as the Prosecution. Your Honour, that is exactly why I explained that the Prosecution had five years time to prepare their case and to prepare the 65 ter list. They had five years, we had a much shorter time, and the rights of the Defence are absolutely different to those of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now -- where is that? In terms of the decision of the Trial Chamber of the 24th of July, 2007, adopting guidelines on the admission and presentation of evidence and conduct of counsel in court, at paragraph 1 of the annex, the guide lines goes as follows, in part: The Trial Chamber requires the parties to inform it of the calling order of witnesses at the end of every week for the coming two weeks. Furthermore, the parties shall inform the Trial Chamber five works days in advance of any changes to the calling order. Moreover the parties shall provided a list of documents which they intend to use for the examination-in-chief of each witness, at least two workings days before the start of the testimony and there is no similar guideline relating to cross-examination. I think we will have to go to the guidelines that we have read, together with the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. That being the case at this stage, the think the document is allowed to be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If exhibit -- or document P06261 [sic] can please be shown --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it 61 or 63.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 63.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hubo, I see this is up before the screen in B/C/S and now I see that the English is also there. We can see the name here is Abdelilah Karrache born 27/1/66 in Morocco. Now that is your signature at the bottom, is it sir?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is certificate bearing my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And we can also see that this indicates this person has been a member of the El Mujahid Detachment that is VJ 5689, since 18/8/1994. And this is exactly the same as the information which is on the document that we just saw, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it is the same because I can't recall what it said earlier, but this certificate was issued by the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So this would indicate, sir, that there was information available about the El Mujahid Detachment, at least at the time this was signed?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was information in the shape and form that I described earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And I just have one addition ideal document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And could this please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document is admitted as exhibit number 1316.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would request a written decision by the Trial Chamber connected to the latest decision that it has issued, and we would please request that we be given authorisation to appeal this decision of the Trial Chamber, because I think that this decision of the Trial Chamber is against the fundamental right of the accused and that it is an encroachment of Article 23 of the Statute --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, Article 20.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And therefore I would ask to be certified to appeal, to give a certification to appeal this decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will consider your application and will give you a response in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The document -- with the leave of Mr. President, could the witness please be shown document P06261.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Hubo, you mentioned at various times there were various efforts, including in November 1995, in an attempt to gather information about El Mujahid Detachment.

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now we can see from this document, sir, that that is your signature at the bottom. It is identical to the signatures that we've seen already.

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And we can see that it is dated Zenica, 14 November 1995.

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: We can also see that upon -- it reads upon the inside into the personal record of the Zenica unit, VJ 5023/1 it has been established that El Aref Abd El Lah Mohamed, born on 25/5/1971 in Egypt has been a member of the Zenica unit VJ 5689 since 1 May 1993 until further notice. It also indicates that it will be used for regulating status issues and cannot be used for other purposes. So, Mr. Hubo, in November 1995 you did have good information at least about certain members of the El Mujahid Detachment, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had information that we received from that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: But, again, sir, you're certifying this as true and correct. It contains a stamp and it also has your signature. You wouldn't have done that unless you knew that the document that you have signed is true and accurate?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the top, if you're able to see that, in the heading, specifically line 3 it says: "Pursuant to the Law on The General administrative Procedure," the public body had to respond to somebody's application for information and it also says that having reviewed the documentation we had, it was on that basis that we issued this certificate. In other words, solely on the basis of the information we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions, Your Honour. I do actually, sorry, Your Honour, wish to tender this into evidence, that is P06261.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will become Exhibit 1317.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Robson, any re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Just a few questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hubo, you were shown exhibit 114 which related to certificates. This was a document that had your signature at the bottom. First of all, do you know who prepared that list?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's see ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could quickly bring up exhibit 114.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I would note, Your Honour that this was a document admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'm grateful. If we could please -- let's see, perhaps Mr. Hubo can answer the question without us bringing the document up.

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was produced mainly by individuals from three departments. I can't give you their names, because the fluctuation of staff was very high. Such a document required the involvement of many more people covering many areas of activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And the information that we saw in that document, do you know where that information came from?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information came from the database that we had in relation to that unit. Solely on that basis. It was based on such information received by the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And you mentioned that three departments were involved in the preparation of the list. Do you know if anybody involved in preparing the list was able to verify the information that was passed over to you?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We weren't in a position to verify the information and that was the essential point. We were compelled to copy the data we had. It was for this reason that the commission was formed. Let me state that none of the individuals involved offered any money in relation to that. It was due to the situation in which our services were at the time that such records were kept. The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina only later on formed a council of ministers which investigated matters such as how it came about that some individuals were granted citizenship. I would need much more time to be able to answer this question of yours. But, believe me, we simply didn't have ways of obtaining information and whatever ways we had at our disposal we used them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And it was put to you that on the basis of that list, thousands of marks were paid out to these men. Do you know, were the amounts of money mentioned in marks specified in the list, were they actually paid out to those persons whose names were contained in the list?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. That is a leading question in that the form of it suggests the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any response.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I disagree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Objection overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Can you answer the question, Mr. Hubo? Do you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess actually the witness answered this question under cross-examination. He said certificates were given.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So certificates were issued. Do you know whether thousands of Deutschemarks were paid to these men who were named in the list?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you will allow me, Mr. President, this question by the Prosecutor, struck me as insinuating that I had been paying money out to these individuals. I have to stress, that I didn't pay the money or the commission. It was something that was given by the state. These certificates, more or less, fell through. I have to tell you that the coast of these certificates was two per cent. If you had 10.000 marks due to you under the certificates, you were able to sell the certificate to the funds that were eventually set up for some 100 maximum 200 marks. Therefore, their value corroded and one was not able to use them as was initially intended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's not go to the value. Let me just make one or two points before I hand you over to Mr. Robson. If you got the impression that the Prosecutor was suggesting that you paid them the money, I think that was the wrong impression all you were saying was you certified that those figures were due to those people and therefore the state had to make those payments. And you explained, if I heard you well, that they didn't get the cash but they got certificates in the place of the cash, whatever the value of the certificate after some time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Hubo, I would like to ask you about the document P6263, which was admitted as exhibit 1316.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Could we just quickly bring this up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hubo, do you know where the information came from that has been included within this document, so that the details relating to the name, date of birth, and other pieces of information relating to this Mr. Karrache.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The information contained here was solely taken from the database that we had, and which had been made by the El Mujahid unit. We didn't have any other sources. We weren't able to go out into the unit to inspect this. We were compelled to rely on the extent of the information provided to us by the units. That's the gist of it. All the other documents that are mentioned, including the ones that are disputable were formed on that basis. I want to make that quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And you were asked by the Prosecution whether through this certificate, you were holding out that the information was true and accurate. If we look at this document, do you say at any stage, or do you warrant at any stage that the information contained therein is true and accurate?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you tell me which document you're referring to, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: The document on the screen in front of us.

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to repeat yet again. The document was made on the basis of the information we received from that unit, and it was in no way possible to verify the contents thereof. And that's the gist, the most important bit of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Hubo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a small question, Witness. You told us that sometimes companies or the servicemen had to fight were directly paid by their company. You told us that sometimes people who were in the service were actually paid by their company. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You understood me correctly. But those were rare cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, okay, not very often. Now, did this also happen for volunteers? Could it happen that volunteers would be paid by another source than the funds that the military had?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't talk about that. I can tell you about the Zenica Iron Works, that particular company, because I had contacts with the people who worked there. I'm not competent to speak of other issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But this company paid servicemen, paid people who were in the military.

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, there were rare cases where the company would, in a way, assist its former staff member or worker who was now active in the army. They would send them out packages of foodstuffs or even money. The times were difficult. There were no salaries and it was more of an assistance provided to the worker and his family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But also to the military, to the soldiers directly. Not just to his family but also to the soldier himself?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that way, the member of the army was also more relaxed, knowing that his family back home had food to eat, unlike others who had to leave home without knowing whether his family would be able to make a living and survive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that. And there's another thing I wanted to know. Of course it was very difficult when the armija was created. But obviously there was not enough resources, but I thought I understand that business companies where people worked before the war before they were actually called into the service continued to pay -- to pay -- instead of paying the state they would pay the -- their workers so that they could fight in the armija. Did I understand this correctly or not?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN HUBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such cases of assistance, albeit it rare, by those who could provide it and were willing to provide it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Judge? Mr. Robson, any questions arising from Judge Lattanzi's questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Hubo, this brings us to the end of your testimony. Thank you very much forever taking the time out from your schedule to come and testify at the Tribunal. We hope can you go back home now and join your family. I know that you had to spend the weekend here this last weekend, and at least we now came to the end of your testimony. Are you now excused and you may now leave. Travel well back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may stand down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The matter is postponed to tomorrow at quarter past 2.00. Court adjourned -- 9.00? I beg your pardon, is it 9.00. 9.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 18th day of March, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.
